title: Provenance: following the paper trail
summary: How ownership histories are built, why gaps matter, the special scrutiny of 1933–1945 — and how documents get faked too.

shots.title:
Every painting
has a biography.
shots.narration: Provenance is a work's biography: who owned it, when, and how we know. A strong provenance is hard to fake. A weak one is where most frauds live.

shots.heading: Where the trail is written
items: Inventory numbers on the work itself
shots.narration: The trail is written in contemporary descriptions, collection inventories, numbers painted or stamped on the work itself, and auction catalogues.

shots.text: Gaps aren't proof of fraud. **But they're where fraud hides.**
shots.narration: Most old works have gaps; records get lost. But gaps are where stories get inserted: an anonymous collector, a forgotten storage unit, a client who never existed.
One period gets special scrutiny. Museums such as the National Gallery pay particular attention to where works were between 1933 and 1945 — the years of Nazi confiscation.
In 1998, 44 states endorsed the non-binding Washington Principles on Nazi-confiscated art, starting with a duty to identify art never returned. Best Practices followed in 2024.

shots.text: Labels, stamps and archives **can be forged too**.
shots.narration: Documents can be faked like paintings. Beltracchi used a gallery label of a kind the collection never used; Drewe planted false records inside museum archives.
In the Campendonk case, a court found the auction house had neither checked the provenance it was given nor had the painting scientifically examined before the sale.

shots.text: Search the stolen-art databases **before** you buy.
shots.narration: Basic due diligence includes stolen-art databases. INTERPOL's free ID-Art app, launched in 2021, lets anyone search almost 57,000 registered stolen objects.

shots.text: Grade every link: **documented, weak, or red flag**.
shots.narration: In the lab you'll audit a chain of ownership as a researcher would: grade each link as documented, weak or a red flag, and see where the gaps fall.

steps.title: Provenance audit
steps.brief: Here is the ownership history offered with the case-file portrait. Grade each link: **documented** (independent records tied to this object), **weak** (plausible but unproven) or **red flag** (a specific reason for suspicion). Then check your audit and save it to your casebook.

items.owner: Painted for a Haarlem brewer's family
items.record: Only an ink inscription on the back of the panel names the family. No inventory, will or letter survives.
items.why: An inscription can be added at any time; without a document from the period it is a lead, not proof.

items.record: No record of any kind for eighty years.
items.why: Gaps are common in old provenances. They lower confidence but are not evidence of fraud on their own.

items.record: His probate inventory lists 'a portrait of a woman by the Haarlem master' — no size, no description.
items.why: A vague inventory entry could fit many pictures; without dimensions or a description it can't be tied to this panel.

items.owner: Bought at auction; then by descent in one family
items.record: An 1850 sale catalogue gives the matching subject and dimensions; the lot number is still stencilled on the back; family inventories of 1890 and 1925 list it.
items.why: Independent documents that match the object, plus a number on the work itself, make a strong link.

items.record: No name and no documents. The seller says it 'went to Switzerland for safekeeping'.
items.why: An anonymous owner across 1933–45 is exactly the gap museums must investigate: it can hide confiscation, a forced sale, or an invented history.

items.record: A famous dealer's label on the frame — but the dealer's surviving stock books do not list the picture.
items.why: A label without matching records recalls the fake 'Sammlung Flechtheim' labels in the Beltracchi case. Labels are easy to make.

items.record: A typed certificate of authenticity signed by an expert who died decades ago.
items.why: A certificate adds no new evidence and can be forged — de Hory's dealer copied experts' stamps.

questions.prompt: Which period do museums scrutinise most closely in a provenance?
questions.explain: The years of Nazi confiscation; the National Gallery pays particular attention to where its paintings were then.

questions.prompt: Why can't a label or certificate settle a provenance on its own?
options: Both can be forged, and neither proves that an earlier owner held this object
questions.explain: Fake labels and copied experts' stamps both appear in famous cases.

questions.prompt: In the Campendonk sale, what did the court find the auction house failed to do?
options: Check the provenance or have the painting examined scientifically
Photograph the back of the frame
questions.explain: It relied on the consignor's story and the label.
